newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian dollar rallies on economic strength.
newsitem.headline: Canadian dollar rallies on economic strength.

text.p: The Canadian dollar has soared more than two U.S. cents so far this year and could hit 75 U.S. cents this week on the way to its highest level in almost three years, currency analysts predicted on Thursday.
"We definitely have a shot at it," said Reid Farrill, corporate foreign exchange adviser at brokerage CIBC-Wood Gundy Inc.
Economists said this week's rally could propel the dollar to 75.75 U.S. cents within the next week. The dollar has not been that high since February 1994.
The Canadian currency was trading at 74.70 U.S. cents on Thursday after rising half a U.S. cent on Wednesday.
The surge comes amid heightening domestic and international investor confidence in the Canadian economy, which is expected to show much stronger growth this year.
"We're pretty bullish on the Canadian economy," said Doug Porter, senior economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns.
Nesbitt forecast that Canada's economy would grow by 3.3 percent this year versus an estimated 1.4 percent in 1996.
Canadian traders expected the Bank of Canada to intervene in the market to smooth the dollar's rise, but said the central bank was unlikely to cut interest rates to try to halt the rally.
"I don't think we're at that point in terms of the strength in the Canada (dollar) where a cut in rates is a possibility as yet," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at Bank of Montreal.
Some economists predicted the Bank of Canada would let the currency rise to 80 U.S. cents this year without cutting interest rates.

The Canadian dollar last flirted with the top of its 72 to 75 U.S. cent range on Nov. 7, 1996. The next day the Bank of Canada trimmed short-term interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point, sparking a fall in the currency over the following two months to a low of 72.69 U.S. cents on Jan. 2.
Economists said Canada's brighter economic outlook was restraining the Bank of Canada from a further rate cut.
"We're getting new evidence that maybe growth is moving to a higher level and as a result there just doesn't seem to be a need to ease overall monetary conditions," said Bank of Montreal's Ferley.
The stronger dollar was seen benefiting the Canadian consumer, but was less of a blessing for exporters, who have accounted for most of Canada's growth in the past two years.

"They've (exporters) had an easy ride from the currency for a long time now," said Anita Lauria, economist at Salomon Brothers in New York. "The question really is how quickly do manufacturers continue to respond on the cost side."
